newsitem.title: BOSNIA: British command ends in Bosnia.
newsitem.headline: British command ends in Bosnia.

text.p: Britain's three-year command of international ground forces in Bosnia will end on Wednesday when Lieutenant-General Sir Michael Walker leaves Sarajevo, NATO sources said on Tuesday.
The ground force command was passed from British generals Michael Rose to Rupert Smith under the U.N. mandate, then on to Walker under NATO. Each had his own headquarters in Bosnia.
Another Briton, Lieutenant-General Roddy Cordy-Simpson, will replace Walker.

But a major reorganisation will leave Cordy-Simpson serving as Deputy Commander, Operations, under U.S. General William Crouch, who took control of all NATO-led peace forces in Bosnia earlier this month.

The ground force job which gave Rose and Smith one of the highest military profiles in the world had already become less visible under NATO because the U.S. imposed a layer of command above Walker in Sarajevo.
"For political reasons the Americans insisted on having a four-star in Sarajevo above the ground commander," explained a Western diplomat in the Bosnian capital.

"It was not the best arrangement. It has taken some of the glory out of the ground commander's job. On the positive side, it left the Americans to take more of the heat of public opinion and gave Walker freedom to get on with his mission."

Walker reported to a four-star U.S. admiral with overall command of NATO forces in Bosnia, but the two men had separate headquarters and staffs. Under Crouch the two headquarters have been telescoped into one.

NATO sources report that the integration of what had been two separate commands and the multi-national nature of the NATO effort will bring more than 25 Brigadiers and Generals into NATO's Sarajevo headquarters.
Walker got high marks from the soldiers who served above and below him, and even from Bosnian government officials who have often criticised commanders of international forces.
U.S. Admiral Leighton Smith, overall commander of NATO peace forces in Bosnia until August of this year, regularly went out of his way to praise Walker to reporters.
Walker, born in Rhodesia in 1944, returns to his post as commander of NATO's ACE Rapid Reaction Corps in Germany.

Deployed under the terms of the Dayton peace agreement in December of 1995, he brought more than 50,000 ground troops from 36 countries into Bosnia and achieved most of the tasks laid out in the accord's military annexe in three months.

Under Walker's direction the country's three warring armies were separated and their troops and weapons returned to barracks and cantonment areas, essential first steps towards lasting peace after 43 months of war.
Perhaps the darkest moments in Walker's tenure came in the first three months of 1996 as Serbs burned and looted Sarajevo suburbs which Dayton transferred from Serb to Moslem control.
Critics argue Walker should have dealt aggressively with looters and arsonists and used NATO's superior military force to impose the equivalent of martial law on the suburbs.
Walker's supporters say it would have been a mistake to divert combat troops from the essential work of separating Bosnia's Moslem, Serb and Croat armies.

In his farewell interview Walker told reporters his experience in Bosnia had convinced him of the feasibility of large multi-national interventions provided troops have a clear mandate and chain-of-command and robust rules of engagement.
"I am also a firm believer in the importance of the man on the ground," he said on Monday. "Technology can only take you so far. The individual soldier...has been the hero (in Bosnia)."
